data.title: Indonesia regulator fines and sanctions firms for stock manipulation, disclosure failures
data.description:
[JAKARTA] Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority (OJK) announced on Nov 21 sanctions in 10 capital market violation cases, amid efforts to strengthen enforcement, bolster market integrity and protect investors.

The authority ordered the return of 23.77 billion rupiah (US$1.24 million) in illicit gains from three stock manipulation cases, involving shares of Grand House Mulia, Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur and Suryamas Dutamakmur.

In the Grand House Mulia case, OJK also ordered the closure of 15 securities accounts linked to the trading activity between March and July 2023.

The agency also imposed a total of 3.71 billion rupiah in administrative fines on seven listed companies for disclosure failures, material and affiliated-party transaction breaches, financial reporting violations and non-compliance with share transfer obligations.

OJK also barred multiple individuals involved in the manipulation cases from participating in Indonesia’s capital markets, derivatives and carbon exchange sectors for periods ranging from three to 10 years.

OJK previously sanctioned three listed firms as part of Indonesia’s market reforms following concerns raised by global index providers over the transparency and investability of Indonesia’s capital markets. REUTERS

data.title: Singapore unveils green shipping, AI governance initiatives with China after PM Wong meets Premier Li Qiang
data.description:
[BEIJING] Singapore announced a series of initiatives with China ranging from green shipping to artificial intelligence (AI) governance, as Prime Minister Lawrence Wong wrapped up his visit to the country on Saturday (Nov 21).

The initiatives follow an earlier announcement on Friday that the two countries would begin work on an upgrade to the China-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, known as CSFTA 4.0. 

It also comes after PM Wong met Chinese Premier Li Qiang at the Diaoyutai State Guesthouse, a former imperial garden and modern diplomatic estate, in Beijing.

PM Wong held separate talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Beijing party secretary Yin Li, who is a member of the Communist Party of China’s Political Bureau, a day earlier.

This is PM Wong’s second time meeting Li in Beijing since his introductory visit last year at the Premier’s invitation.

Since then, PM Wong noted that Singapore and China has had a “good, constructive discussion” on how to take the cooperation between both countries forward. 

“Both China and Singapore have continued to build on our All-Round High-Quality, Future-oriented Partnership,” he said.

PM Wong also referenced the upcoming 22nd Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation with China, which will be held in the Republic on Sunday and Monday.

At the event’s conclusion, he said it is expected to yield more than 20 deliverables spanning areas like trade digitalisation and financial integration. It will also include research and innovation in the healthcare and education industries.

“That reflects the depth and breadth of our cooperation,” said PM Wong.

Premier Li said in Mandarin that by joining hands to foster open development, both China and Singapore can “contribute greater positive energy toward stability and prosperity, both within this region and globally”.

“As a long-standing, friendly neighbour, China is prepared to strengthen strategic communication with Singapore,” said Li.

This includes expanding the partnership toward both countries to produce more tangible outcomes, “all while continuing to enhance the friendship between our two peoples”.

The media were allowed to be in attendance only for the first few minutes of the leaders’ meeting.

According to a read out of the meeting from Singapore’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the leaders discussed the opportunities and challenges brought by AI, including the need for international coordination on AI safety and governance. 

They also discussed the potential of cooperating on the practical use of AI in areas like healthcare and manufacturing, that can increase productivity and bring benefits to both countries. 

PM Wong also introduced Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Home Affairs Sim Ann; Minister of State for Manpower and Energy, Trade and Industry Foo Cexiang; and Member of Parliament Hamid Razak.

The meeting with Li capped a series of talks for PM Wong with Chinese leaders after he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting.

On Friday, PM Wong met Chinese President Xi Jinping and spoke of deepening ties between Singapore and China and saw the launch of the China-Singapore Free Trade Agreement 4.0 upgrade. He also met Beijing party secretary Yin Li, a member of the Communist Party of China’s Political Bureau.

In a social media post after meeting Yin, PM Wong described Beijing as a major research and innovation hub and said “there is much that Singapore and Beijing can do together”.

He said they discussed plans to deepen integration across the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. These developments, he added, offer “exciting opportunities” for cooperation in areas ranging from technology and innovation to sustainable development and education.

New areas of cooperation 

In a statement on Saturday, Singapore’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said [insert how MFA links the initiatives to PM Wong’s visit].

Singapore’s Ministry of Transport (MOT) said the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to facilitate the movement of goods and people, improve transport safety and support the rollout of green and digital shipping corridors between Singapore and China.

The agreement also covers intelligent transport systems and AI. 

A committee co-chaired by the transport ministers of the two countries will oversee its implementation and meet every two years, alternating between Singapore and China.

MOT said the MOU builds on the Singapore–PRC All-Round High-Quality Future-Oriented Partnership established in 2023.

Separately, Singapore’s Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) said it also signed an  MOU related to cooperating on green industry development with China’s National Development and Reform Commission ahead of PM Wong’s visit. 

The agreement sets up a framework for policy exchanges, research and industry partnerships in areas including energy efficiency, green upgrading of infrastructure development, and biodiversity conservation, among others.

MSE said it will lead implementation and involve relevant ministries and agencies across the Singapore Government.

The Republic’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology have also mapped Singapore’s AI Verify Testing Framework, which helps organisations validate the technology’s performance, against a Chinese industry standard for managing AI system risks.

IMDA said the comparison shows how safeguards and checks under one framework correspond to those under the other. This could help businesses using both frameworks avoid duplicating some checks.

The two countries are also due to sign an MOU on educational technology and the use of AI in schools on the sidelines of the Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation later this month, Singapore’s Ministry of Education (MOE) said.

The National University of Singapore’s AI Centre for Educational Technologies and East China Normal University’s Shanghai Institute of AI for Education will lead the collaboration.

MOE said it will cover testing tools, sharing AI-enabled teaching practices and developing ways to assess vocational and human skills, along with short exchanges and joint workshops.

The teams behind the Singapore Student Learning Space and the Smart Education of China platform will share how they develop and run their platforms and explore sharing AI literacy resources.

The two countries will also use existing exchanges to strengthen educators’ AI and digital skills, and build on partnerships between their primary and secondary schools, said MOE.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: SoftBankâsÂ Son explored US$1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix: report
data.description:
SOFTBANK Group CEO Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible trillion-dollar “buyout” of South Korean memory chip company SK Hynix, The Information reported on Friday (Nov 20), citing people familiar with the matter.

The Information quoted a SoftBank spokesperson as saying Son was no longer considering such a deal.

“SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration,” the report said, citing the spokesperson.

SK Hynix said in a statement it has no knowledge of the matter described in the Information report.

It added that any foreign acquisition of the company would require prior government approval under Korean law.

A SoftBank spokesperson referred to the statement the company gave to the Information, when Reuters sought a comment. REUTERS

data.title: Chinaâs top planner seeks faster construction of state projects
data.description:
CHINA’S top planning agency urged local authorities to speed up the construction of government investment projects and disbursement of funds in a bid to spur growth in the world’s second-largest economy.

The National Development and Reform Commission also called for stronger monitoring and coordination among local governments to accelerate construction and funding to generate more on-the-ground activity as quickly as possible, it said in a statement posted on its WeChat account on Saturday (Nov 21).

Local authorities were told to step up preparatory work and strengthen strategic planning to improve the quality of projects in the pipeline.

China’s growth weakened across the board last month as investment unexpectedly worsened while consumption and industrial output undershot estimates, in a sign Beijing’s latest stimulus measures have yet to feed through to the economy.

Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1 per cent in the first 10 months of 2026 from the same period last year, lower than the 7 per cent decline expected by economists. In October alone, investment shrank 17 per cent from a year earlier, according to Bloomberg Economics, its sharpest fall outside the Covid pandemic.

NDRC’s latest call follows an August push to stabilise investment, when officials urged faster issuance and use of local government special-bond funds and deployment of new policy-based financing tools.

China recorded about 240 trillion yuan (US$36 trillion) of fixed-asset investment from 2021 through 2025, growing at an average of 2.3 per cent annually, according to an article published on the NDRC website in June. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Ask not what AI can do for you
data.description:
I CONFESS I am old-school.

For years, colleagues and friends have regarded me as someone slow to embrace change, particularly technology. This observation is not entirely misplaced.

Yet something unexpected has happened. I find myself taking to artificial intelligence with an enthusiasm that has surprised even me.

More amusingly, some who once considered me technologically challenged have yet to embrace it to the same extent.

I have been reflecting on this irony. Perhaps our ability to benefit from AI has less to do with technological proficiency and more to do with our willingness to learn, the questions we ask and what we choose to do with the answers.

We have spent considerable time asking what AI can do for us. Let’s reframe that question.

Learning begins with wanting to learn

My work in executive education brings me into conversations with leaders and organisations across industries and geographies. I have come to recognise an important distinction: Teaching someone AI is not the same as making that person want to learn AI.

There is a saying that leadership cannot simply be taught; it must also be caught. Something similar may apply to AI.

In the Singapore Management University’s public programmes, participants who self-enrol often arrive with curiosity and questions. In customised corporate programmes, participants may be nominated by their organisations.

Many are enthusiastic, but others have yet to discover why the learning matters to them.

Increasingly, I see greater value in beginning not with the technology, but with a problem. When participants identify a genuine pain point in their work and explore how AI might help them address it, the learning becomes purposeful. The problem belongs to them, along with the desire to solve it.

Organisations can provide access, tools and training. But they cannot mandate curiosity.

The advantage of youth and the value of experience

I marvel at how effortlessly my son, who works in professional services, uses AI to analyse complex data sets, identify patterns and generate insights for his managers. My younger colleagues display the same fluency.

Watching them, I sometimes wonder whether those who developed expertise the hard way have been overtaken.

When a doctoral candidate recently described how AI was accelerating her research, I felt a twinge of envy. My years of doctoral research were difficult, spent poring over papers, wrestling with competing arguments, and enduring frustration, tears and self-doubt.

Yet, that time taught me something invaluable: to question assumptions, recognise inconsistencies and exercise judgment when answers were elusive.

Today, when AI produces convincing responses in seconds, that experience helps me recognise what is missing and ask better questions.

I do not wish those struggles on today’s researchers. Removing drudgery is progress. But removing the intellectual effort through which judgment develops is another matter.

The challenge is to ensure convenience does not replace thinking.

Real magic happens when the digital fluency of the younger generation meets the lived experience and judgment of the older, creating outcomes neither could achieve as effectively alone.

Where empathy makes the difference

Recently, two friends faced deeply distressing circumstances. One lost a life partner. Another was diagnosed with a terminal illness. In both situations, AI proved useful in helping me navigate unfamiliar terrain, gather information and consider ways of supporting their families.

But there were moments when information alone fell short. AI may suggest words of comfort, but it cannot take our place beside a grieving friend.

At the workplace of our terminally ill friend, senior leaders took time to speak with the family, help them navigate complex arrangements and explore ways to ease their financial burden. Colleagues quietly assumed additional responsibilities.

What moved me was the genuine concern that drove these actions. People chose to go beyond their roles because a colleague and their family needed them.

We often speak of empathy as a soft skill, something desirable but perhaps secondary to intelligence and productivity. I argue otherwise.

Empathy makes us pause before acting, consider another person’s circumstances and recognise that the most efficient solution may not always be the most compassionate one.

AI can help organisations make informed decisions, allocate resources and improve efficiency. But human leaders must still decide what matters, whom their decisions affect and when compassion should take precedence over convenience.

Imagine a world where AI enables us to do more in less time, but we become less willing to give that time to one another. What, then, have we really gained?

Technology can expand our capacity to help. Empathy gives that capacity a human purpose.

The question that matters

Much of public discourse about AI centres on whether machines will replace human beings. The concerns are real. Some jobs will change significantly, and some tasks may disappear altogether.

But our preoccupation with replacement may be distracting us from a more immediate responsibility.

Are we becoming better thinkers because of AI, or merely faster producers of answers? Are we using the time it saves to exercise better judgment, deepen relationships and solve meaningful problems?

I am grateful to be living through this transformation at this life stage. The years spent studying, working, making mistakes and learning from people have given me a foundation from which to engage with AI in ways I could not have earlier. I am also learning from younger colleagues who approach it with admirable openness and confidence.

I will probably remain old-school in many ways. But if that means valuing hard-earned knowledge, sound judgment, human relationships and empathy, I am content to carry those qualities into the new world.

AI may help me accomplish more than I ever imagined. But what I choose to do, why it matters and whose lives I touch remain questions that I must answer for myself.

The writer is head of commercial, executive development, at Singapore Management University

data.title: Anthropic researcher claims to solve Riemann maths problem with Claude
data.description:
ON THE heels of Anthropic PBC’s record-breaking initial public offering, a researcher at the company said he believes he used its artificial intelligence software to solve a famous number theory problem that has plagued mathematicians for more than 150 years.

Mathematician Levent Alpoge published a note on his personal website on Friday (Nov 20), claiming to have come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. He shared a link to code written in the programming language Lean that he said showed evidence of his success. 

According to his note, Alpoge messaged Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei on Sunday night to ask about announcing his findings to the public.

Alpoge called the timing of his announcement “horrible,” but said, “I just could not live if I waited even longer.” Anthropic declined to comment, and Alpoge did not respond to a request to comment.

The Riemann hypothesis relates to the distribution of prime numbers and has long been considered one of the most difficult math problems in the field.

OpenAI and Anthropic have been working for years to demonstrate the advanced capabilities of their most cutting-edge models by solving challenging math and life sciences problems. 

If confirmed, Alpoge’s work would mark the second Millennium Prize Problem that may have been solved by AI; OpenAI said its models had generated a solution to the 90-year-old Navier-Stokes problem in September. 

Andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said he verified Alpoge’s work about the Riemann hypothesis on his computer and has seen at least three other verifications on multiple systems from other professional mathematicians.

Alpöge’s efforts with Claude build on the work of many mathematicians who have studied the Riemann hypothesis, as well as the field of mathematic formalisation, according to Sutherland.

“I am both very nervous and very excited” for the future, Sutherland said, explaining that mathematicians have years ahead to dig into this proof to understand how it can be applied. “This is a day for celebration,” Sutherland said, even as he acknowledged the concerns in his field about AI’s potential impacts the math profession and other jobs.

Noah Giansiracusa, an associate professor of math at Bentley University and faculty associate at Harvard University, added that, if the solution works, it’s a big deal for AI.

“It sounds like there’s a pretty good chance this is airtight and valid,” Giansiracusa said.

Alpoge described the experience of attempting to prove the problem as a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt.” 

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpoge wrote. BLOOMBERG

data.title: AI can manage a familyâs wealth. It cannot decide what the wealth is for
data.description:
WITHIN a few years, artificial intelligence will take over much of the work in managing family wealth.

Consolidating accounts across entities, checking documents against the law, drafting and monitoring agreements, producing reports on every holding – tasks that occupy accountants, lawyers and family office staff are being automated.

Singapore and Hong Kong, where governments have actively courted family offices, will be among the first places to feel the change.

Consider a typical family that owns three operating companies and a portfolio managed by its single family office in Singapore.

A reporting system pulls figures from all of them every morning. Each company is ahead of budget, and the portfolio is performing better than its benchmark. By every measure on the screen, the year is a success.

Yet, the family has agreed that it will buy out two cousins and that the founder may start a new venture. Neither is communicated to the system; nothing says that the next three years must produce cash to fund these decisions.

Each company owned by the family reinvests its profits, as a well-run company should, and the system reports that this is going well because it was not made aware of new requirements.

The family office uses an investment platform that rebalances the portfolio towards its benchmark. The model finds regional property underweight and adds to it. The family’s largest company is a property developer.

Seen from the portfolio’s perspective, the allocation is balanced. Seen from that of the family, its exposure to one market has just gone up disproportionately.

Then a tax tool optimises the group’s structure. It works from the companies’ figures and assumes, as the companies do, that profits are reinvested. Corporate tax falls.

It does not consider tax on dividends because nothing the tool was given says the owners intend to withdraw cash. The plan is optimal for the companies; it is expensive for the family members when they are hit by their tax bill for taking out cash for the buyout and new venture.

Each answer provided by the system is correct. Each system optimises what it was given: the companies’ budgets, the portfolio’s benchmark, the companies’ tax. Each receives its instructions through a different channel.

None of them knows what the owners need, and the whole infrastructure drifts away from the family’s goals.

Compliance, relational, perspective

One way to see where this gap lies is through what I call “the three functions of ownership”: compliance, relational and perspective.

Compliance ensures all aspects of ownership, such as tax and regulatory rules, abide by the law. The law is codified, so much of this task will be automated by AI.

Relational is what the owners agree among themselves: the direction for their wealth, its limits, who acts on their behalf and what is reported back to them. Drafting and monitoring such agreements will also be largely automated, but the agreement itself remains a decision only the owners can take.

Perspective carries the agreement through. It gives each significant investment and business holding a mandate, assesses the strategy proposed to meet it, takes important decisions back to the family and tracks the results.

It does so with the family’s whole wealth in view, optimising within the limits that compliance sets, and, most importantly, reaches the organisation through one channel: the person leading the wealth on the owners’ behalf.

In the hypothetical family above, the chain breaks between the relational and perspective functions.

The owners have an agreement, but it was not decided and written down in the language of perspective. There is nothing to carry through, so each system optimises against the goals of a company or a portfolio instead.

Decisions still rest with the family

Today, an experienced finance director or family office head who knows what the owners want might catch all three concerns: question the reinvestment plans, notice the added property exposure, ask about dividend tax.

AI can do the same analysis, faster and across every holding, but only if the owners’ requirements have been established. Without that, automation does not close the gap. It makes the gap more consequential.

Closing the chain starts with a clearly communicated agreement. The family decides that they need cash over the next three years for the buy out and the venture, that their investment portfolio should factor in their property company, and that their taxes should be optimised for taking money out.

The person leading the wealth then turns that into instructions every system can work from.

Each company gets a mandate for what it must pay out, so its budget includes the cash the owners need.

The investment platform gets a limit on property allocation for the whole wealth, so owning a property developer does not unbalance the portfolio.

The tax tool is told that cash will be paid out, so dividend tax is part of the plan.

With that in place, AI can do what it does best. It flags the conflicts before the budgets are approved, before the platform rebalances and before the tax plan is adopted. The owners’ time is then spent on the decisions that are theirs.

For advisers, the shift is just as large. Much of what is billed today in compliance and relational work will be done by machines. The value that remains lies in helping owners define what the AI should serve.

AI will make it ever easier to produce information, assess alternatives and carry out decisions. None of that establishes what the wealth is supposed to bring the family. That remains with them, and carrying it through requires a function of its own.

The writer is founder of H S Nielsen, which advises owners of complex wealth structures

The commentary is based on the writer’s own experiences, observations and argument. AI tools were used for drafting in English and editing. The writer remains fully accountable for the commentary’s accuracy, originality and final form.
